chapter_summary:
Deploying an ARKit application to an iOS device involves a slightly different workflow compared to Android, primarily due to Apple's stricter ecosystem and reliance on Xcode for the final build and signing process. While Unity handles the initial project generation, Xcode takes over for the crucial steps of code signing, provisioning, and deployment to a physical device.

The fundamental prerequisite for iOS deployment is an **Apple Developer Program** membership. This is a paid annual subscription that grants you access to developer tools, allows you to sign applications, and submit them to the App Store. Without it, you can develop and test on simulators, but deploying to a physical device for anything beyond basic development often requires a valid developer account and associated provisioning profiles. You'll also need a Mac computer with **Xcode** installed, as it's the primary IDE for iOS development and the gateway to managing your developer certificates and provisioning profiles.

In Unity, the initial steps mirror Android's: ensure you have **iOS Build Support** installed via Unity Hub. Then, go to `File > Build Settings` and switch your platform to "iOS." This will re-import assets for the iOS target. Next, navigate to `Edit > Project Settings > Player`. Under the iOS tab (the Apple icon), you'll configure several critical settings. Just like Android, you'll set your `Company Name`, `Product Name`, and importantly, the `Bundle Identifier` (e.g., `com.cohortia.arkitdetector`). This identifier must be unique across all iOS apps and directly corresponds to the App ID you'll manage in your Apple Developer account. Set the `Target Minimum iOS Version` to an appropriate value (ARKit requires iOS 11 or later). Ensure `Scripting Backend` is set to `IL2CPP` and `Architecture` is `ARM64`.

A crucial step for ARKit applications is configuring privacy settings. Apple requires explicit declarations for privacy-sensitive features. For AR, this means camera access. In Unity's Player Settings, under the iOS tab, expand "Other Settings" and scroll down to "Camera Usage Description." You *must* provide a user-friendly string here, explaining why your app needs camera access (e.g., "Used for augmented reality experiences to place virtual objects in your environment."). If this is missing, your app will likely crash on launch when trying to access the camera, or be rejected from the App Store.

For XR capabilities, enable the **ARKit** provider under the iOS tab in `Edit > Project Settings > XR Plug-in Management`. This ensures the necessary ARKit frameworks are included in your Xcode project.

Once these settings are configured, go to `File > Build Settings`, ensure your scenes are checked, and click "Build." Unity will ask for a folder to save the Xcode project. Create a `Builds/iOS` folder in your project root. Unity will then generate an Xcode project within this folder. This process can take a significant amount of time, especially for larger projects.

After Unity finishes, open the generated `.xcodeproj` file in Xcode. This is where the real iOS deployment work begins. In Xcode, select your project in the Project Navigator. Then, in the main editor area, go to the "Signing & Capabilities" tab. Here, you'll select your "Team" (your Apple Developer account). Xcode will then attempt to automatically manage your **provisioning profiles** and **signing certificates**. If you have a valid developer account and have configured it in Xcode's preferences (`Xcode > Settings > Accounts`), this process is usually smooth. Xcode will create or fetch the necessary profiles and certificates to sign your app. Common mistakes here involve incorrect bundle identifiers that don't match your App ID in the developer portal, or expired provisioning profiles.

Finally, connect your iOS device to your Mac via USB. Select your device from the scheme selector dropdown next to the "Run" and "Stop" buttons in Xcode. Then, click the "Run" button (the play icon). Xcode will compile your project, sign it, and deploy it to your connected device. The first time you deploy to a new device, you might need to trust your developer account on the device itself (`Settings > General > VPN & Device Management > Developer App`).

Debugging on iOS devices typically involves using Xcode's console output and debugger. You can also use `Console.app` on macOS to view device logs, similar to `adb logcat`. For more advanced debugging and profiling, Xcode's built-in Instruments tool is invaluable, allowing you to analyze performance, memory usage, and graphics rendering on the device. Remember to always test your ARKit application on a physical device, as the AR experience cannot be accurately simulated.

screens.title: Building and Deploying to iOS (ARKit)
screens.subtitle: From Unity project to AR experience on a physical iPhone or iPad

narration.text: In this lesson we'll make a complete pathway from a Unity AR project to a running ARKit app on an iOS device. You will learn the account prerequisites you must hold, the Unity Player Settings that must be correct, how Unity generates an Xcode project, and the Xcode steps for signing and deploying to a physical device. Along the way we'll emphasize the mandatory privacy text for camera access and explain why code signing and provisioning are a unique part of Apple's workflow. For a concrete example, imagine preparing a simple AR plane detection scene in Unity, switching the platform to iOS, setting the bundle identifier to com. cohortia. arkitdetector, enabling ARKit in XR Plug-in Management, then building an Xcode project and using your Apple Developer Team to sign and run on a test iPhone. A common misconception is assuming Unity alone completes the build — but in reality Xcode performs the final signing and device deployment. By the end of this module you will be able to generate the Xcode project, resolve signing errors related to bundle IDs and profiles, and deploy your ARKit app for testing. Keep in mind the clear purpose strings and hardware requirements for AR testing when you prepare to build.

narration.text: These objectives focus your practical work for iOS ARKit deployment. First, you will understand the account and hardware prerequisites, because without a valid Apple Developer membership and a Mac with Xcode you cannot sign or deploy apps to a physical iOS device. Second, you'll learn to configure the Unity Player Settings correctly — bundle identifier, minimum iOS version, scripting backend, and architecture — since mismatches here are the most common cause of Xcode signing and runtime errors. Third, you'll practice generating a clean Xcode project from Unity and inspecting its structure so you can locate the Info. plist and check that your Camera Usage Description is present. Fourth, you'll become familiar with enabling the ARKit XR plug-in so that required frameworks are included. Each of these skills matters because deploying AR requires both Unity-side configuration and Xcode-side signing. Together they reduce wasted build time and avoid rejections or runtime crashes due to missing privacy strings or wrong architectures.

screens.title: Apple Developer Program & Why It Matters
screens.subtitle: Membership, certificates, and provisioning explained

narration.text: The Apple Developer Program is the gate that allows you to sign and distribute iOS apps. Membership is an annual subscription that gives you access to certificates, App IDs, and the ability to deploy to physical devices beyond the simulator. Practically, this means that without an active developer account you can still develop and test in Unity and the iOS simulator, but you cannot install signed builds on most real devices or publish to the App Store. For example, when a student tries to deploy an AR app to their iPhone and sees a signing error, the most likely cause is an expired membership or a missing provisioning profile tied to their account. A common misconception is that a free Apple ID is sufficient to run apps on a personal device; Apple’s policies permit limited device testing in some scenarios, but reliable deployment and App Store distribution require the paid program. The key takeaway is that signing and provisioning are identity and permission systems: certificates prove who you are, App IDs bind your bundle identifier, and provisioning profiles link those certificates to specific devices. Before building, verify your account in Xcode under Settings → Accounts and confirm your Team is listed. Consider this membership the single point of control that enables Xcode to create signing materials and allow your AR experience to run on real hardware.

keyIdea.title: Why a Developer Account?
keyIdea.text: An Apple Developer membership provides the certificates and provisioning profiles needed to sign apps, authorize devices, and publish to the App Store.

content.html:
Core Concept
Apple Developer Program
Paid annual membership that enables app signing, device provisioning, and App Store distribution.
• Certificates verify the developer’s identity to Apple and devices.
• App IDs (tied to bundle identifiers) determine which services an app can use.
• Provisioning profiles tie certificates and App IDs to specific devices for testing.
Key Takeaway

Without an active Apple Developer membership, you cannot reliably sign and run ARKit apps on physical devices or submit them to the App Store.

Concept Cards
Certificates
Digital proof of developer identity used in signing.
App ID
Registered identifier that maps to your bundle identifier and entitlements.
Provisioning Profile
Links certificate, App ID, and allowed devices for testing.
Common Mistake
Expired membership or mismatched bundle identifier causes signing failures.

screens.title: Configuring Unity Player Settings for iOS
screens.subtitle: Bundle ID, target iOS, scripting backend, architecture, and camera usage

narration.text: Configuring Unity’s Player Settings is a practical step that directly affects the generated Xcode project. Begin by installing iOS Build Support via Unity Hub if you haven't already. In Unity select File, Build Settings, and switch platform to iOS to re-import assets for the target. In Edit, Project Settings, open Player and select the iOS icon. Set Company Name and Product Name, then set a unique Bundle Identifier such as com. cohortia. arkitdetector; this must match the App ID you register in the Apple Developer portal. Choose a Target Minimum iOS Version of 11.0 or later because ARKit requires iOS 11+. Under Scripting Backend set IL2CPP and set Architecture to ARM64 to match modern devices and App Store requirements. One crucial, frequently overlooked field is Camera Usage Description under Other Settings. Provide a clear human-facing reason like “Used for augmented reality experiences to place virtual objects in your environment.” If missing, the app will likely crash when accessing the camera or be rejected from review. After these settings are in place, ensure your AR scene is added to Build Settings before clicking Build. A common misconception is thinking default values are sufficient; explicit architecture and iOS target decisions avoid build-time errors and runtime crashes on devices. Check these settings each time you switch branches or import a package that may alter Player Settings.

keyIdea.title: Player Settings matter
keyIdea.text: Correct bundle ID, IL2CPP, ARM64, minimum iOS version, and Camera Usage Description prevent signing mismatches and runtime camera crashes.

content.html:
Process Flow
Configure Player Settings
Step-by-step checklist to avoid common iOS build problems.
  1. Install iOS Build Support via Unity Hub.
  2. File → Build Settings → Switch Platform → iOS.
  3. Edit → Project Settings → Player → set Company, Product, Bundle Identifier.
  4. Set Target Minimum iOS Version to 11.0 or higher, Scripting Backend to IL2CPP, Architecture to ARM64.
  5. Under Other Settings add Camera Usage Description string.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly set iOS target, backend, and camera permission text before building — defaults can cause device crashes or App Store rejection.

Example: Bundle Identifier & Info
Example Bundle ID
com.cohortia.arkitdetector
Camera Usage
"Used for augmented reality experiences to place virtual objects in your environment."
Common Mistake
Leaving Scripting Backend at Mono or Architecture at Universal can produce incompatible binaries for modern devices.

screens.title: Enabling ARKit and Generating the Xcode Project
screens.subtitle: XR Plug-in Management and Unity Build to Xcode

narration.text: Enabling ARKit in Unity is the bridge that ensures ARKit frameworks are included in the generated Xcode project. Open Edit, Project Settings, XR Plug-in Management, choose the iOS tab, and check the ARKit provider entry. Unity may prompt to install the ARKit package; accept and let the package install. With ARKit enabled, confirm your AR scenes are marked in File, Build Settings. When you click Build, Unity asks for a folder; create a Builds/iOS folder in your project root and save there. Unity will then produce an Xcode project that contains targets, frameworks, and an Info. plist derived from your Player Settings. This generation step can take several minutes for larger projects because Unity compiles shaders and links native plugins. A common misconception is that toggling ARKit in packages is optional — it is required for frameworks to appear in Xcode, or the project will fail to link ARKit symbols. After generation, open the. xcodeproj in Xcode and inspect the project navigator. Look for Unity-iPhone target, Info. plist, and Frameworks. Confirm that a Camera Usage Description string exists in Info. plist. If you must repeat a build, prefer a clean folder to avoid stale artifacts. This step hands the baton to Xcode, which performs the signing and deployment steps you will perform next.

keyIdea.title: Enable ARKit
keyIdea.text: ARKit provider must be enabled in XR Plug-in Management so Unity includes required frameworks in the generated Xcode project.

content.html:
Process
Enable ARKit & Build
  • Edit → Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management → iOS → check ARKit provider.
  • Install any prompted ARKit packages via Package Manager.
  • File → Build Settings: ensure your AR scene is checked.
  • Click Build and save into a fresh Builds/iOS folder.
Build Note
Generation produces a Unity-iPhone Xcode project containing targets, frameworks, and Info.plist entries based on your Player Settings.
Example: Build Folder Structure
Builds/iOS/
Unity-iPhone.xcodeproj Unity-iPhone/Info.plist Frameworks/ Libraries/
Key Takeaway

Generate the Xcode project into a clean Builds/iOS folder so you can open it in Xcode and complete signing and deployment.

screens.title: Understanding the Generated Xcode Project
screens.subtitle: Targets, Info.plist, frameworks, and build artifacts

narration.text: Once Unity finishes, the Xcode project organizes your app into familiar iOS build constructs. The main target is usually Unity-iPhone; it contains build phases, linked frameworks, and settings that determine the final binary. Info. plist houses runtime metadata such as the Camera Usage Description you provided in Unity’s Player Settings. Frameworks and Libraries folders include ARKit and other native frameworks necessary for runtime. The project navigator shows source files, assets, and build settings — important places to confirm Bundle Identifier and deployment target. Understanding this structure helps when resolving linking errors or missing entitlements. For example, if AR symbols fail to link, inspect Build Phases to ensure ARKit framework appears under Link Binary With Libraries. A common misconception is that the generated project is only for archiving; in fact you must use Xcode to set the Team for signing, manage provisioning, and choose a device target for deployment. Treat the Unity-generated project as the handoff artifact: Unity sets up scenes and build settings, while Xcode resolves signing, linking, and device-specific deployment. Before running, double-check that the Bundle Identifier in Xcode matches the App ID registered in your Apple account and that the Info. plist contains the camera usage string. This inspection step prevents many signing and runtime issues during the first deployment.

keyIdea.title: Xcode project is the handoff
keyIdea.text: Unity prepares source and settings, but the Xcode project contains targets, Info.plist, and framework links that Xcode will compile, sign, and deploy.

content.html:
Architecture
Xcode Project Structure
Targets
Unity-iPhone target drives build settings and signing.
Info.plist
Contains Camera Usage Description and other runtime keys.
Frameworks
ARKit and system frameworks linked during build.
Quick checks before deploying:
  • Bundle Identifier matches App ID in developer portal.
  • Info.plist contains Camera Usage Description.
  • ARKit framework appears under Link Binary With Libraries.
Example: Info.plist excerpt
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Used for augmented reality experiences to place virtual objects in your environment.</string>
Common Mistake

Assuming Unity will resolve signing; in truth you must open Xcode to choose Team and resolve provisioning.

screens.title: Signing & Provisioning in Xcode
screens.subtitle: Selecting Team, automatic provisioning, and resolving errors

narration.text: Signing and provisioning are the iOS-specific steps that tie your identity, app identifier, and devices together. Open the generated Xcode project, select the Unity-iPhone project in the Project Navigator, and select the main target. In the Signing & Capabilities tab choose your Team — this is the Apple Developer account configured in Xcode’s preferences. If Allow Xcode to manage signing is checked, Xcode will attempt to create or download the required provisioning profiles and certificates. If Xcode reports an error, read it carefully: common causes are a mismatched bundle identifier that doesn’t exist in your App IDs, expired certificates, or a missing device in the provisioning profile. For example, if your bundle identifier is com. cohortia. arkitdetector but the developer portal only has com. cohortia. myapp registered, Xcode cannot match the App ID and will show a signing error. A helpful workflow is to confirm your Apple ID is added under Xcode → Settings → Accounts, then return to Signing & Capabilities to refresh profiles. If needed, manually create an App ID in the developer portal and ensure it includes the same bundle identifier. Remember that provisioning profiles link your certificate and allowed device UDIDs; if your device is not included, deployment will fail. After Xcode successfully manages signing, you are ready to select a connected device and run the app.

keyIdea.title: Signing essentials
keyIdea.text: Choose your Team in Xcode and let Xcode manage provisioning; fix bundle identifier mismatches and expired certificates to resolve signing errors.

content.html:
Process
Signing & Provisioning
Steps and checks to prepare your app for deployment to devices.
  1. Open the generated .xcodeproj in Xcode and select the main target.
  2. Go to Signing & Capabilities and select your Team (Apple Developer account).
  3. Enable Automatic signing to let Xcode create provisioning profiles.
  4. If errors appear, verify Bundle Identifier matches an App ID in your developer portal.
  5. Ensure your device UDID is included in the provisioning profile for testing builds.
Example: Common error
"Signing for 'Unity-iPhone' requires a development team. Select a development team in the Signing & Capabilities editor." — typically indicates no Team is selected or the account is not added to Xcode.
Troubleshooting
Add your Apple ID in Xcode Preferences → Accounts, refresh profiles, match bundle ID, or create App ID in developer portal.
Key Takeaway

Automatic signing will solve most cases; address bundle ID mismatches and expired profiles when Xcode reports signing errors.

screens.title: Deploying to a Physical iOS Device
screens.subtitle: Device selection, trust flow, and first-run checks

narration.text: Deploying to a device is the final physical verification step for ARKit. Connect your iPhone or iPad to the Mac via USB and unlock it. In Xcode’s scheme selector choose the connected device from the dropdown. Press Run; Xcode will compile the app, sign it with the selected Team, and attempt to install it on the device. If this is the first time you deploy from this Team, you might see an alert on the device to trust the developer. On the device go to Settings, General, VPN & Device Management and trust the developer app. After installation, launch the app and confirm AR behaviors such as plane detection and object placement. If the app crashes immediately, check that the Camera Usage Description exists in Info. plist — missing permission strings commonly cause crashes when the app attempts to access the camera at startup. Another common issue is architecture mismatch; ensure the build is for ARM64 and not for simulator-only architectures. For logging during deployment use Xcode’s console to view device logs live; this helps you identify permission denials or runtime exceptions. Treat the first device run as a checklist: trust the developer, allow camera permission, observe ARKit initialization, and confirm expected scene behavior.

keyIdea.title: Device deployment
keyIdea.text: Select your connected device in Xcode, run the build, trust the developer on the device if needed, and verify AR functionality and camera permissions on first launch.

content.html:
Process
Deploy to Device
  1. Connect device via USB and unlock it.
  2. Select device from Xcode scheme selector and press Run.
  3. If prompted on device, go to Settings → General → VPN & Device Management and trust the developer.
  4. Allow camera permission when requested and observe AR initialization.
First-run checks
  • Camera permissions prompt appears and accepts the usage string.
  • AR plane detection initializes without immediate crashes.
  • Xcode console shows no missing framework or signing errors.
Example: Trust flow
On first install from your Team, the device will require you to trust the developer profile under VPN & Device Management to run unsigned apps from that account.
Pro Tip
Keep Console.app open on macOS to capture device logs if the app closes instantly after launch.

screens.title: Unity vs Xcode Responsibilities
screens.subtitle: What Unity handles and what Xcode must complete

narration.text: Understanding which tool is responsible for each part of the workflow prevents confusion and wasted time. Unity is responsible for preparing scenes, assets, and platform-specific Player Settings. Unity includes frameworks via the XR plug-in system and generates the Xcode project containing targets, frameworks, and an Info. plist inferred from your Player Settings. Xcode, by contrast, is responsible for compiling native code for the device architecture, performing code signing with certificates and provisioning profiles, linking system frameworks like ARKit, and deploying to connected hardware. For instance, Unity cannot sign an iOS binary with your Apple Developer certificate — that must be done in Xcode. A frequent misconception is expecting Unity’s Build button to be the final step. In reality, Build hands off a project that still needs Xcode to set the Team, resolve provisioning, and run on a device. Think of Unity as the authoring and packaging tool and Xcode as the final compiler, signer, and deployment interface. When troubleshooting, determine whether failures occur before or after the handoff: build-time shader or asset issues belong in Unity, while signing, linking, and device install errors are Xcode’s domain.

keyIdea.title: Division of labor
keyIdea.text: Unity prepares and packages the AR project; Xcode compiles, signs, links frameworks like ARKit, and deploys to the device.

content.html:
Comparison
Unity vs Xcode
Unity
Author scenes, set Player Settings, enable ARKit plug-in, generate Xcode project.
Xcode
Compile for device, sign with certificates, manage provisioning, deploy and debug on hardware.
Quick diagnostic: If the build fails before generating Xcode, fix Unity settings. If signing or device install fails, inspect Xcode’s Signing & Capabilities.
Analogy
Unity prepares the package and paperwork; Xcode is the delivery truck that must be licensed and permitted to drive onto the customer's property.
Common Misconception

Thinking a Unity Build is sufficient to run on device without opening Xcode and resolving signing and provisioning.

screens.title: Camera Usage Description and Info.plist
screens.subtitle: Why this string is required and how it's represented

narration.text: The Camera Usage Description is a user-facing string required by Apple whenever an app requests camera access. For ARKit apps this is mandatory because AR requires the camera to view the real world. You enter this text in Unity under Player Settings → iOS → Other Settings → Camera Usage Description. Unity copies that string into the generated Info. plist under the NSCameraUsageDescription key. If the string is missing the app may crash when trying to access the camera or be rejected during App Store review. For example, a suitable value is: Used for augmented reality experiences to place virtual objects in your environment. A misconception is to add a terse or technical string; instead use a clear, concise explanation the user will understand. In the Xcode project you can inspect Info. plist to verify the key exists. Below is a small excerpt showing how the key appears in Info. plist after generation. If you ever need to change it after building, update the Player Settings and regenerate, or edit Info. plist before building in Xcode. Always verify this string appears exactly as you intend because it will be shown in the permission prompt on the device.

keyIdea.title: Privacy string required
keyIdea.text: NSCameraUsageDescription must be present with a clear user-facing message or the AR app may crash or be rejected.

content.html:
Definition
Camera Usage Description
This human-readable string tells users why your app needs camera access and appears in the system permission prompt.
When missing, attempts to access the camera can crash the app or cause App Store review rejections. Keep the message simple and relevant to the AR experience.
Info.plist excerpt
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Used for augmented reality experiences to place virtual objects in your environment.</string>
Pro Tip
Author the message for clarity. It is what users see when they first allow camera access.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Build and Deploy an ARKit Xcode Project
screens.subtitle: Follow the checklist to produce a working AR app on device

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough guides your lab practice: first confirm prerequisites — a Mac with Xcode, an active Apple Developer Program membership, and an AR-capable iPhone or iPad connected by USB. In Unity switch to iOS in File → Build Settings and confirm your AR scene is checked. In Player Settings fill Company and Product names, set Bundle Identifier to a unique value like com. cohortia. arkitdetector, set Target Minimum iOS Version to 11.0 or later, choose IL2CPP as the Scripting Backend and ARM64 for Architecture, and add a Camera Usage Description. Next enable ARKit in Edit → Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management. Then click Build and create a Builds/iOS folder for the generated project. Open the. xcodeproj in Xcode, choose your Team under Signing & Capabilities and allow Xcode to manage signing. Connect your device, select it in the scheme, and press Run. If Xcode complains about provisioning or signing, double-check that your bundle identifier exists as an App ID in the developer portal and that your device UDID is included in your provisioning profile. On first install trust your developer profile on the device under Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. Launch the app and verify AR plane detection and object placement. This lab reinforces the full workflow and highlights common fixes for signing and permission issues.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Follow the checklist from Player Settings through Xcode signing to deploy and verify ARKit functionality on a real iOS device.

content.html:
Practice Lab
Build & Deploy Checklist
Prerequisites
Mac + Xcode, Apple Developer account, AR-capable device.
Unity Setup
Switch to iOS, set bundle ID, IL2CPP, ARM64, camera string.
Build & Open
Build to Builds/iOS, open .xcodeproj in Xcode.
Deployment Steps
  1. Select Team under Signing & Capabilities and enable automatic signing.
  2. Connect your device and choose it as the run destination.
  3. Click Run in Xcode and accept trust on the device if prompted.
  4. Verify camera permission and AR plane detection on launch.
Troubleshooting
If you see signing errors, check bundle id matches App ID, account is in Xcode Preferences → Accounts, and device UDID is enrolled in the provisioning profile. Use Xcode console to read runtime errors.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts you need for iOS ARKit deployment. First, the Apple Developer Program is a paid annual membership that gives you certificates and provisioning profiles necessary to sign and distribute apps. Second, Xcode is the Mac O S IDE that compiles, signs, and deploys the generated project to devices; it is required for final signing and debugging. Third, the Bundle Identifier is the unique app string that must match the App ID registered in your developer portal; mismatches here commonly block signing. These three ideas form the backbone of iOS deployment: account and certificates, the Xcode toolchain, and the identifier that ties your app to Apple’s services. Keep these concepts in mind as quick checks when you hit errors during build or deployment. If signing fails, inspect these points first before deeper debugging.

keyIdea.title: Memory snapshot
keyIdea.text: Apple Developer membership, Xcode, and a correct Bundle Identifier are the minimum foundation for successful iOS ARKit deployment.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Key Concepts
Apple Developer Program
Paid subscription granting signing certificates, App IDs, and provisioning profiles needed for device deployment and distribution.
Xcode
Apple’s IDE used to open the Unity-generated project, manage signing, and deploy to devices.
Bundle Identifier
A unique reverse-domain string that maps your app to an App ID in the developer portal for signing and entitlements.
Summary

Confirm membership, Xcode configuration, and correct bundle ID first when diagnosing iOS deployment errors.

narration.text: Here are three more compact concepts to keep top of mind when deploying ARKit apps. First, the Camera Usage Description must be present and human readable in Info. plist, otherwise camera access will fail or the app may be rejected. Second, set Scripting Backend to IL2CPP and Architecture to ARM64 in Unity’s Player Settings to produce device-compatible binaries; simulator-only architectures will not run on hardware. Third, use Xcode’s Signing & Capabilities to select your Team and let Xcode manage provisioning profiles; when signing errors appear, verify bundle ID, team membership, and profile expiration. These short checks compose a practical preflight: camera permission, build architecture, and signing configuration. Make them a routine part of every iOS AR build so you spend less time troubleshooting and more time testing your AR experience on real devices.

keyIdea.title: Practical preflight
keyIdea.text: Before building, confirm camera usage text, IL2CPP + ARM64 settings, and Xcode Team/signing configuration to avoid common runtime and signing problems.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Key Concepts
Camera Usage Description
NSCameraUsageDescription is required and visible to users when requesting camera permission.
IL2CPP & ARM64
Use IL2CPP and ARM64 to build device-compatible native code for modern iOS hardware.
Xcode Signing Checks
Select Team, inspect provisioning profiles, and resolve bundle ID issues in Signing & Capabilities.
Final Takeaway

Perform a preflight: confirm camera string, IL2CPP + ARM64, and signing setup before each iOS AR build to minimize failures.
